passage:
"Bhaiya, do you have the twelve-shade marker set?" Dolma asked the stationery shopkeeper. He gave a slow side-to-side head wobble and kept counting change.
"Is that a yes?" whispered Anirban, who had just arrived from abroad.
"Could be yes. Could be okay, I heard you. Could be maybe," Dolma whispered back. "His face is friendly, but he didn't say a word."
"So what do we do?"
"We ask." She turned. "Bhaiya, is the set in stock right now, or should I check another shop?"
"Tomorrow morning, new stock," he said, smiling.
"So that was neither yes nor no," Anirban said as they stepped out.
"It was 'come back tomorrow'," she grinned.

qa.q: What did Dolma ask the shopkeeper for?
qa.a: She asked for the twelve-shade marker set.

qa.q: What did Anirban think the head wobble meant, and how does Dolma explain it?
qa.a: Anirban is unsure whether it means yes, and Dolma says it could be yes, okay, I heard you or maybe. Her whispered comment about his friendly face shows she does not want to guess.

qa.q: What could Anirban try next time he sees a head wobble?
qa.a: He could ask a short clarifying question, like whether the item is in stock right now, instead of assuming agreement or refusal.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper see his own head wobble?
qa.a: He probably sees it as a friendly, everyday acknowledgement and not as a puzzling signal at all.

grounding: A head wobble carries mixed meaning in India, and a clarifying question sorts it out.

passage: Last summer I, Ujjwal, asked my uncle Kishore if I could borrow his old cycle for the week. He nodded his head sideways in that slow wobble and went on reading the paper. I thought, great, that's a yes. The next morning I wheeled the cycle out of his shed and rode to my friend's house. When I got back, he was standing at the gate, not angry, just confused. "I only said I'd think about it," he said. I felt hot in the face. I realised the wobble had meant I heard you, not go ahead. We laughed about it later. Now when I see one, I ask, "So is that okay for today?" It only takes five seconds.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal ask uncle Kishore to lend?
qa.a: Ujjwal asked to borrow Kishore's old cycle for the week.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal think the head wobble meant, and how did Ujjwal feel on learning Kishore's meaning?
qa.a: Ujjwal took it as a yes, but Kishore only meant he would think about it. Ujjwal felt embarrassed, hot in the face, on realising the mismatch.

qa.q: What would you advise Ujjwal to do the next time?
qa.a: Ask a short, friendly follow-up question before acting, such as whether it is okay for today.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt when he saw the cycle was gone?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and puzzled rather than angry, since he had not yet decided. 🙂

grounding: A head wobble and mixed signals lead to a misreading, and a clarifying question is the remedy.

passage:
Observation note - Chandrika Menon, Class 11 Chemistry, international school
Chetan joined this term from Pune. On Monday I asked him if his lab report was finished and he gave a quick head wobble with a small smile. I read it as yes and moved on.
On Wednesday the report still wasn't in. I nearly marked it late, but I remembered the wobble and wondered if I had read it wrongly.
I asked him after class, "When you did this," and I copied the wobble, "did you mean yes, or something else?" He laughed. "Ma'am, it meant 'I heard you, I'm on it.' Half done."
Since then I ask a second question when I'm not sure: "Is that a yes, or not yet?" He answers straight away. Two other students have started doing the same with each other.

qa.q: When did Chandrika first ask Chetan about his lab report?
qa.a: Chandrika asked him on Monday if his lab report was finished.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling and meaning when he wobbled, and how could it have been read another way?
qa.a: He meant "I heard you, I'm on it," with the report half done, and he seemed calm and at ease about it. Chandrika had read the same wobble as a plain yes.

qa.q: What small step did Chandrika add to avoid the mix-up?
qa.a: She now asks a clarifying question such as "Is that a yes, or not yet?" whenever a wobble or nod leaves her unsure.

qa.q: What would change if Chandrika had marked the report late without asking?
qa.a: Chetan would likely have felt unfairly judged, since in his mind he had never promised it was finished, and the misunderstanding would have stayed hidden.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a head wobble meaning "I hear you" rather than yes, and a listener checking with a clarifying question.

passage:
Thursday
Big lesson today, diary. Last night I asked Pankaj bhaiya if he could collect my blouse from the tailor on his way back from college, because the function is on Saturday. He was eating and did the head wobble. I went to sleep happy.
Today at five I asked for it. Blank face. "I never said yes! I said maybe, if I finished early." He didn't finish early.
I was so angry I nearly cried, and I told him his head says yes even when his mouth says nothing. He said, "My head said 'hmm, let's see.'" Honestly, we were both a bit right.
So we went together on his scooter, and the tailor had it ready anyway. 😅
Rule for me from now: wobble means ask again. "Yes-yes, or maybe?"
- Alka

qa.q: What did Alka ask Pankaj to collect?
qa.a: Alka asked him to collect a blouse from the tailor on his way back from college.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling on finding out the blouse wasn't collected?
qa.a: Alka was angry and upset, close to tears, after going to sleep sure it was a yes. Writing that they were both a bit right shows Alka later felt calmer and saw the misunderstanding.

qa.q: What would you advise Alka to do next time someone wobbles in reply?
qa.a: Ask a quick follow-up, like the diary's own "Yes-yes, or maybe?", before counting on the answer.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have seen the conversation?
qa.a: Pankaj seems to have meant a relaxed "let's see" while eating, so he may have felt blamed for a promise he never thought he made.

grounding: The diary shows a head wobble meaning maybe being read as yes, and the writer deciding to check with a clarifying question.

passage: The afternoon bus to Hubballi had just pulled out, leaving dust over the tea stall where Jatin was stacking glasses. Rekha came by with her little brother, carrying a bundle of stitched blouses back from the tailor. "The fair committee meets tomorrow at the temple hall," Jatin said. "We need someone for the rangoli stall. Will you come?" Rekha tilted her head side to side, a soft wobble, and smiled a little. Jatin almost wrote her name on his list. Then he remembered last year, when his cousin had read the same wobble as yes, and Rekha never came. He put the pencil down. "Is that a yes, or a maybe?" Rekha laughed. "It means I heard you. I have to ask Amma, she might need me at home." "Tell me by the evening bus?" Another wobble, quicker this time, with a firm nod at the end. "Yes. That one is yes."

qa.q: What was Rekha carrying?
qa.a: Rekha was carrying a bundle of stitched blouses back from the tailor.

qa.q: Why did Jatin put the pencil down instead of writing Rekha's name?
qa.a: Jatin felt unsure and a bit wary, remembering last year when his cousin read the same wobble as yes and Rekha never came. The wobble could mean yes, maybe or just 'I heard you'.

qa.q: What small step helped Jatin avoid a wrong guess?
qa.a: Jatin asked a plain clarifying question, 'Is that a yes, or a maybe?', and then set a clear time to confirm by the evening bus. 🙂

qa.q: What might Rekha have wanted Jatin to understand about the first wobble?
qa.a: Rekha wanted Jatin to know it meant she had heard him but needed to ask Amma first, so it was neither a yes nor a no yet.

grounding: It shows a head wobble in a small-town setting meaning 'I heard you' rather than yes, and a listener checking with a clarifying question instead of assuming.
